The most recent quarterly application-layer test, completed in June 2026, identified one high-severity finding related to insufficient rate limiting on a password reset endpoint in the newly launched international mobile application; remediation was completed within the 30-day SLA and confirmed through retest. An open risk item involves the staging environment's configuration drift relative to production for the international markets, which the security engineering team has flagged as potentially limiting the effectiveness of staging-based testing for those corridors until infrastructure- as-code parity is achieved, targeted for Q1 2027.

author: Ciara Miller
text:
Risk Management Policy (RSK-001) | 1. Purpose/Summary
This Risk Management Policy establishes Veridian Dynamics' enterprise risk management framework, defining risk categories, assessment methodology, appetite statements, and governance structures used to identify and manage risks across the organization. The policy applies to all departments and covers operational, financial, compliance, technology, strategic, and reputational risk categories, and is owned by the Enterprise Risk Management function within Operations.

author: Ciara Miller
text:
Risk Management Policy (RSK-001) | 2. Background/Context
Ciara Miller, Head of Enterprise Risk Management, oversees the risk program, which reports quarterly to the Board Risk Committee. The framework was substantially revised in 2024 to adopt a standardized 5x5 risk matrix across all departments, replacing inconsistent department-specific scoring methods that made enterprise-level risk aggregation difficult. This version 2.4 incorporates a new risk appetite statement approved by the Board in December 2024, which for the first time sets quantitative thresholds for operational loss tolerance tied to the company's fraud and operational risk programs.

author: Ciara Miller
text:
Risk Management Policy (RSK-001) | 3.1 Risk Categories and Ownership
Six risk categories are defined: operational, financial, compliance, technology, strategic, and reputational. Each category has a designated risk owner at the department-head level who is responsible for maintaining a risk register and reporting material changes to Enterprise Risk Management monthly.

author: Ciara Miller
text:
Risk Management Policy (RSK-001) | 3.2 Assessment Methodology
Risks are scored on a 5x5 matrix evaluating likelihood and impact, each on a 1-5 scale, producing a composite score from 1 to 25. Risks scoring 15 or above are classified as high and require a documented mitigation plan with assigned owner and target date, reviewed monthly by Enterprise Risk Management until closed or reduced below the high threshold.

author: Ciara Miller
text:
Risk Management Policy (RSK-001) | 3.3 Risk Appetite Statement
The Board-approved risk appetite statement sets an operational loss tolerance of no more than 0.15% of annual revenue from combined fraud, operational error, and processing-failure losses. Compliance risk appetite is set at zero tolerance for willful regulatory violations, with a low tolerance for inadvertent violations provided they are self-identified and remediated within committed timelines.

author: Ciara Miller
text:
Risk Management Policy (RSK-001) | 3.4 Governance and Reporting
Enterprise Risk Management maintains a consolidated enterprise risk register, reviewed monthly by the Compliance Committee and quarterly by the Board Risk Committee. Any risk scoring 20 or above triggers an immediate out-of-cycle notification to the Chief Risk Officer regardless of the regular reporting cadence.

author: Ciara Miller
text:
Risk Management Policy (RSK-001) | 4. Key Details
Risk scoring model: 5x5 matrix (likelihood x impact), max score 25
High-risk threshold: Score of 15 or above
Immediate escalation threshold: Score of 20 or above
Operational loss tolerance: 0.15% of annual revenue
Compliance risk appetite (willful violations): Zero tolerance
Risk register review cadence: Monthly (Compliance Committee), Quarterly (Board)
Risk categories: 6 (operational, financial, compliance, technology, strategic, reputational)

author: Ciara Miller
text:
Risk Management Policy (RSK-001) | 5. Exceptions, Risks, or Open Issues
Enterprise Risk Management has identified that the new 0.15% operational loss tolerance threshold has not yet been reflected in the loss-reserve methodology described in the Fraud Program Documentation (FRD-001), which uses a different reserve calculation basis. A reconciliation project is planned for the next policy cycle to ensure consistent treatment across documents. Additionally, the planned Digital Asset product line is expected to introduce a new risk subcategory (digital asset custody and volatility risk) that is not yet addressed in the current risk taxonomy; Enterprise Risk Management has recommended this be incorporated before any production launch.

author: Aubrey Graham
text:
Sanctions Program (SAN-001) | 1. Purpose/Summary
This document describes Veridian Dynamics' Sanctions Program, established to ensure compliance with OFAC regulations and other applicable sanctions regimes. The program governs screening of customers, counterparties, and transactions against designated sanctions lists, and establishes roles and responsibilities within Legal & Compliance for managing potential matches. It covers onboarding screening, ongoing monitoring, and transaction-level interdiction across the peer-to-peer payment platform.

author: Aubrey Graham
text:
Sanctions Program (SAN-001) | 2. Background/Context
As a money services business operating a peer-to-peer payment platform, Veridian Dynamics is subject to U.S. sanctions laws administered by the Office of Foreign Assets Control, as well as equivalent regimes in jurisdictions where the company holds money transmitter licenses. The Sanctions Program was first formalized in 2022 when the company's user base crossed 1 million active accounts, triggering enhanced regulatory scrutiny under state money transmitter examinations. Legal & Compliance subsequently licensed a third-party screening tool, WatchTower Screen, to automate list-matching rather than relying on manual lookups, which had proven unworkable at scale. The program has been updated twice since initial adoption, most recently to incorporate the Sectoral Sanctions Identifications (SSI) List and to formalize the sanctions officer role, currently held by Aubrey Graham, who reports to the Chief Compliance Officer. The program is reviewed at least annually and whenever OFAC issues material regulatory guidance affecting money services businesses.

author: Aubrey Graham
text:
Sanctions Program (SAN-001) | 3.1 Screening Scope and Lists
WatchTower Screen checks customers and transaction counterparties against the OFAC Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List, the Sectoral Sanctions Identifications List, the Consolidated Sanctions List, and relevant United Nations and EU sanctions lists for cross-border transfers. Screening occurs at three points: account opening, any change to customer profile data (name, address, date of birth), and in real time at transaction initiation for every transaction regardless of dollar amount.

author: Aubrey Graham
text:
Sanctions Program (SAN-001) | 3.2 Real-Time Transaction Screening
Every transaction submitted on the platform is screened against active sanctions lists in real time prior to settlement, with an average screening latency of 150 milliseconds. Transactions involving a potential name match are held automatically pending review by a sanctions analyst; no transaction may settle while a potential match is outstanding.

author: Aubrey Graham
text:
Sanctions Program (SAN-001) | 3.3 Match Review and Disposition
Potential matches are reviewed using a documented match-scoring methodology that considers name similarity, date of birth, and geographic indicators. Analysts must document a clear rationale for any match disposition, whether true match, false positive, or inconclusive requiring escalation to the Sanctions Officer.

author: Aubrey Graham
text:
Sanctions Program (SAN-001) | 3.4 Governance and Reporting
The Sanctions Officer reports program metrics, including match volume, false-positive rate, and any blocked-property reports filed with OFAC, to the Chief Compliance Officer monthly and to the Board Risk Committee quarterly.

author: Aubrey Graham
text:
Sanctions Program (SAN-001) | 4. Key Details
Screening tool: WatchTower Screen
Screening trigger points: Account opening, profile change, every transaction
Screening timing: Real-time, pre-settlement
Average screening latency: 150 ms
Lists covered: OFAC SDN, SSI, Consolidated, UN, EU
Sanctions Officer: Aubrey Graham
Reporting cadence: Monthly (CCO), Quarterly (Board Risk Committee)

author: Aubrey Graham
text:
Sanctions Program (SAN-001) | 5. Exceptions, Risks, or Open Issues
A known limitation of the current implementation is that cross-border transfers routed through certain regional banking partners are screened by the partner's own system in addition to WatchTower Screen, creating occasional discrepancies in match disposition that require manual reconciliation. Legal & Compliance is also monitoring proposed OFAC guidance on digital-asset-adjacent payment rails, which could expand screening obligations if Veridian Dynamics' planned Digital Asset features move forward. No sanctions violations have been identified during the current program cycle; two inconclusive matches remain open pending additional documentation from the account holders involved.

author: Ronaldinho
text:
Sanctions Risk Assessment (SAN-002) | 1. Purpose/Summary
This Sanctions Risk Assessment evaluates Veridian Dynamics' inherent and residual sanctions risk exposure across its customer base, product offerings, and geographic footprint. It is conducted annually by Legal & Compliance to inform the design of the Sanctions Program (SAN-001) and to satisfy regulatory expectations that money services businesses maintain a documented, risk-based approach to sanctions compliance. The assessment assigns risk ratings to customer segments and recommends control enhancements where residual risk remains elevated.

author: Ronaldinho
text:
Sanctions Risk Assessment (SAN-002) | 2. Background/Context
Ronaldinho, Sanctions Risk Manager, led the 2025 assessment with input from Operations, Finance, and the product team responsible for the planned Digital Asset features. The assessment methodology follows a standard inherent-risk times control-effectiveness model, scoring each customer segment and product line on a 1-5 scale across geographic risk, customer type risk, and product risk, then applying a control effectiveness discount based on the maturity of existing screening controls. This year's assessment is notable for incorporating, for the first time, a dedicated risk category for cross-border remittance corridors following the platform's expansion into three new international markets in Q2 2025. The prior assessment, conducted in 2024, rated overall residual sanctions risk as 'Moderate'; this year's assessment reflects a reassessment of screening cadence assumptions based on actual operational practice observed during a Q2 2025 internal audit walkthrough of the screening process.

author: Ronaldinho
text:
Sanctions Risk Assessment (SAN-002) | 3.1 Methodology
Inherent risk scores are calculated per customer segment using geographic exposure, transaction velocity, and product complexity. The existing customer base, now exceeding 3.1 million accounts, is segmented into domestic retail users, domestic small-business users, and cross-border remittance users, each scored independently.

author: Ronaldinho
text:
Sanctions Risk Assessment (SAN-002) | 3.2 Screening Cadence Finding
The audit walkthrough confirmed that new transactions are screened at initiation, but that the existing customer base is re-screened against updated OFAC SDN list additions through a nightly batch process that runs at 11:00 PM Eastern Time, rather than continuously in real time as originally designed. This means a customer added to the SDN list earlier in the day could retain account access for up to several hours before the nightly batch reconciliation flags the profile. The assessment recommends evaluating a move to intraday incremental list-update checks to close this gap.

author: Ronaldinho
text:
Sanctions Risk Assessment (SAN-002) | 3.3 Geographic Risk
The three new international markets entered in Q2 2025 were each rated using the Basel AML Index and relevant FATF mutual evaluation reports as reference points, resulting in two markets rated 'Medium' inherent risk and one rated 'Medium-High' due to limited correspondent banking transparency.

author: Ronaldinho
text:
Sanctions Risk Assessment (SAN-002) | 3.4 Overall Rating and Recommendations
Overall residual sanctions risk is rated 'Moderate-High' for 2025, an increase from 'Moderate' in 2024, driven primarily by the cross-border expansion and the batch re-screening finding. Recommendations include closing the nightly batch gap, enhancing geographic risk scoring for future market entries prior to launch, and increasing Sanctions Officer staffing from one to two full-time analysts.

author: Ronaldinho
text:
Sanctions Risk Assessment (SAN-002) | 5. Exceptions, Risks, or Open Issues
The most significant open issue identified in this assessment is the discrepancy between the Sanctions Program's documented real-time screening design and the nightly batch process actually observed for existing-customer re-screening. Legal & Compliance has opened a remediation item to either update SAN-001 to accurately reflect the batch cadence or to invest in engineering work to achieve true real-time re-screening against list updates. A target remediation date of Q4 2025 has been proposed to the Chief Compliance Officer but is not yet formally approved. Additional recommended staffing increases are pending Finance budget approval.

SOC 1 Type I Report (SOC-001) | 1. Purpose/Summary
This SOC 1 Type I Report presents an independent auditor's examination of the design of internal controls at Veridian Dynamics relevant to user entities' internal control over financial reporting, as of a point in time: December 1, 2025. The report was prepared by Hartwell & Finch LLP in accordance with AT-C Section 320 and covers controls within the transaction processing, settlement, and general ledger reconciliation environments supporting the peer-to-peer payment platform.

author: External Auditor (Hartwell & Finch LLP)
text:
SOC 1 Type I Report (SOC-001) | 2. Background/Context
Veridian Dynamics engaged Hartwell & Finch LLP to perform its first SOC 1 Type I examination in late 2025 in response to requests from several enterprise partners and banking counterparties who require assurance over financial-reporting-relevant controls before integrating with the platform. This Type I report evaluates whether controls were suitably designed as of the specified date but does not test operating effectiveness over a period, which is instead addressed in the subsequent SOC 1 Type II Report (SOC-002) covering a later review period. The examination scope was defined jointly by Finance and the external auditor and covers five control objectives spanning transaction initiation, authorization, processing, and reconciliation to the general ledger maintained in QuickBooks.

author: External Auditor (Hartwell & Finch LLP)
text:
SOC 1 Type I Report (SOC-001) | 3.1 Scope and Control Objectives
The examination covers five control objectives: (1) transaction authorization and authentication, (2) accurate transaction processing and posting, (3) completeness of settlement with banking partners, (4) timely and accurate general ledger reconciliation, and (5) restricted access to financial systems including QuickBooks and the core ledger database.

author: External Auditor (Hartwell & Finch LLP)
text:
SOC 1 Type I Report (SOC-001) | 3.2 Description of the System
Transactions initiated on the platform flow through an authorization service that validates account status and available balance, then post to an internal ledger before being batched for settlement with banking partners on a T+1 basis. Daily settlement totals are reconciled against QuickBooks general ledger entries by the Finance Operations team using an automated reconciliation tool.

author: External Auditor (Hartwell & Finch LLP)
text:
SOC 1 Type I Report (SOC-001) | 3.3 Control Design Findings
The auditor concluded that controls across all five objectives were suitably designed as of December 1, 2025, with one exception noted: access recertification for QuickBooks users was found to rely on an informal quarterly email confirmation process rather than a system-enforced recertification workflow, which the auditor flagged as a design gap relative to leading practice, though not a failing of the stated control objective.

SOC 1 Type II Report (SOC-002) | 1. Purpose/Summary
This SOC 1 Type II Report presents Hartwell & Finch LLP's examination of both the design and operating effectiveness of Veridian Dynamics' internal controls relevant to user entities' financial reporting, over the review period of January 1, 2026 through June 30, 2026. This report builds on the control environment first described in the SOC 1 Type I Report (SOC-001) and provides enterprise partners with assurance that the described controls operated effectively throughout the six-month review period, not merely at a single point in time.

author: External Auditor (Hartwell & Finch LLP)
text:
SOC 1 Type II Report (SOC-002) | 2. Background/Context
Following the Type I examination completed in January 2026, Finance management committed to remediating the single design exception identified at that time, related to QuickBooks access recertification. Ahead of this Type II review period, Finance implemented a system-enforced quarterly access recertification workflow integrated with the identity management platform, replacing the prior informal email-based process. This Type II report evaluates whether this and all other previously examined controls operated effectively throughout the six-month period, based on sample testing performed by Hartwell & Finch LLP across each month of the review period.

author: External Auditor (Hartwell & Finch LLP)
text:
SOC 1 Type II Report (SOC-002) | 3.1 Scope and Testing Approach
The auditor tested the same five control objectives examined in the Type I report, using monthly samples of transactions, reconciliations, and access change records. Sample sizes ranged from 25 to 45 items per control per month depending on population size and control frequency.

author: External Auditor (Hartwell & Finch LLP)
text:
SOC 1 Type II Report (SOC-002) | 3.2 Access Recertification Remediation Testing
The auditor confirmed that the new system-enforced quarterly access recertification workflow was implemented effective February 1, 2026, and operated effectively for the two recertification cycles falling within the review period, with no exceptions noted in either cycle.

author: External Auditor (Hartwell & Finch LLP)
text:

Four of the five control objectives operated effectively throughout the entire review period with no exceptions. One exception was noted within the settlement completeness control objective: in March 2026, a batch settlement file reconciliation was delayed by 3 business days due to a banking partner system outage, resulting in a temporary reconciliation backlog that was fully cleared once the partner system was restored. The auditor determined this was an isolated environmental event rather than a control design or operation failure, but it is disclosed as an exception per professional standards.

author: External Auditor (Caldwell Assurance Group)
text:

Production access requires multi-factor authentication and is provisioned through a role-based access control model administered in the identity management platform. Transaction Monitoring Documentation (TXM-001) | 1. Purpose/Summary
This document describes the automated transaction monitoring system used to support Veridian Dynamics' AML Program (AML-001), detailing the rule library, alert generation thresholds, and analyst review workflow. The system, named PulseWatch, is maintained by a dedicated Transaction Monitoring team within Legal & Compliance, led by Jonas Whitfield, and generates alerts that feed into the SAR evaluation process.

author: Robert Lewandowski
text:
Transaction Monitoring Documentation (TXM-001) | 2. Background/Context
PulseWatch was implemented in 2022 and has undergone several rule-tuning cycles to balance alert volume against analyst capacity. Robert Lewandowski, Transaction Monitoring Manager, leads quarterly rule effectiveness reviews, adjusting thresholds based on alert disposition data to reduce false positives while maintaining detection coverage. This version 2.8 update reflects the most recent quarterly tuning cycle, completed in June 2026, which recalibrated the primary structuring-detection rule threshold based on twelve months of disposition data showing an elevated false-positive rate at the previous setting.

author: Robert Lewandowski
text:
Transaction Monitoring Documentation (TXM-001) | 3.1 System Overview
PulseWatch evaluates every transaction against a rule library of 38 active rules covering structuring, rapid movement of funds, dormant account reactivation, and velocity-based anomalies, among others. Rules operate in parallel, and a single transaction may trigger multiple alerts.

author: Robert Lewandowski
text:
Transaction Monitoring Documentation (TXM-001) | 3.2 Primary Structuring Detection Threshold
The primary structuring-detection rule generates an alert when a customer's transactions aggregate to $10,000 or more within a rolling 24-hour period, based on the June 2026 tuning cycle's recalibration from the prior $7,500 threshold, which disposition data showed was generating a disproportionate volume of false positives relative to confirmed structuring patterns at current transaction volumes.

author: Robert Lewandowski
text:
Transaction Monitoring Documentation (TXM-001) | 3.3 Alert Review Workflow
Alerts route to a queue reviewed by Transaction Monitoring analysts, who have 5 business days to disposition each alert as either closed with no further action, escalated for SAR evaluation to the AML Compliance Officer's team, or referred for additional information gathering from the customer.

author: Robert Lewandowski
text:
Transaction Monitoring Documentation (TXM-001) | 3.4 Rule Effectiveness Reviews
Quarterly rule effectiveness reviews analyze each rule's alert volume, escalation rate, and confirmed-SAR rate, with underperforming rules (escalation rate below 2%) flagged for threshold recalibration or retirement consideration.

author: Robert Lewandowski
text:

System name: PulseWatch
Active monitoring rules: 38
Primary structuring alert threshold (current): $10,000 / rolling 24 hours
Prior structuring alert threshold: $7,500 / rolling 24 hours
Alert review SLA: 5 business days
Rule effectiveness review cadence: Quarterly
Underperforming rule escalation-rate flag: Below 2%

author: Robert Lewandowski
text:
Transaction Monitoring Documentation (TXM-001) | 5. Exceptions, Risks, or Open Issues
The Transaction Monitoring team has not yet completed a formal reconciliation of the $10,000 automated structuring-alert threshold against the $5,000 manual SAR evaluation threshold documented in the AML Program Documentation (AML-001); the two figures serve related but distinct purposes (automated alert generation versus manual evaluation criteria for transactions however identified), but Jonas Whitfield has flagged internally that the gap between the two thresholds merits a joint review with the AML Compliance Officer to confirm no detection coverage gap exists between $5,000 and $10,000. This review is tentatively planned for the next quarterly rule effectiveness cycle but has not been formally scheduled. Separately, PulseWatch's rule library has not yet been extended to cover the three new international markets' distinct transaction patterns, which the team is monitoring closely for emerging typologies.

Website Design Documentation (WEB-001) | 1. Purpose/Summary
This document describes the design standards and architecture of the Veridian Dynamics public-facing website, which serves as the primary channel for consumer sign-up, product marketing, help center content, and legal disclosures. It covers the content management approach, accessibility standards, and required legal disclosure placements, and is maintained by the Web Platform team within Operations in coordination with Legal & Compliance for disclosure content.

author: Neymar
text:
Website Design Documentation (WEB-001) | 2. Background/Context
Neymar, Head of Web Platform, led a full redesign of the website in 2024, migrating from a legacy content management system to a modern headless CMS architecture to improve page load performance and support the three new international markets' localization requirements. The redesign project included a comprehensive accessibility audit, conducted by an external accessibility consultancy, which informed updated design standards targeting WCAG 2.1 Level AA conformance across all public pages. This version 2.0 update reflects the completed migration and the addition of localized site versions for the three new markets, launched progressively between April and June 2026.

author: Neymar
text:
Website Design Documentation (WEB-001) | 3.1 Content Management Architecture
The website runs on a headless CMS with content authored by the marketing and legal teams and rendered through a custom front-end application. Legal disclosure content, including the Website Terms of Service (WEB-002) and the Consumer Terms and Conditions (CMP-004), is managed in a dedicated legal-content workspace requiring Legal & Compliance sign-off before any publish action.

author: Neymar
text:
Website Design Documentation (WEB-001) | 3.2 Accessibility Standards
All public pages target WCAG 2.1 Level AA conformance, validated through automated scanning on every deployment and a manual accessibility review conducted quarterly by the external consultancy. The 2025 audit identified 34 accessibility issues, of which 31 have been remediated as of this document's publication.

author: Neymar
text:
Website Design Documentation (WEB-001) | 3.3 Required Disclosure Placements
Legal & Compliance requires that links to the Website Terms of Service, Consumer Terms and Conditions, and Privacy Policy appear in the website footer on every page, and that fee schedules be displayed prominently on any page referencing transfer pricing, consistent with state money transmitter advertising regulations.

author: Neymar
text:
Website Design Documentation (WEB-001) | 3.4 Localization
The three new international market site versions are maintained as separate locale branches within the same CMS, with legal disclosure content translated and reviewed by local counsel before publication, distinct from the primary English-language legal content workspace.
